title: Nexus Appliances: warranty provision and loss contingencies (probable, reasonably possible, remote)
participant_role: Corporate controller at Nexus Appliances preparing Year 1 year-end entries for warranties and legal claims
judge_role: Vice president of sales at Nexus Appliances, who wants to record only actual repair costs and ignore lawsuits until they are decided

difficulty.rationale: Warranty provision plus probable, reasonably possible and remote contingencies.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of corporate controller for NEXUS APPLIANCES, a manufacturer of kitchen appliances. The vice president of sales (judge) has asked you to explain the Year 1 year-end accounting for product warranties and for several legal claims against the company.

This year NEXUS APPLIANCES launched a high-end smart blender and sold $500,000 of units. To build consumer confidence, the vice president of sales (judge) offered a 1-year comprehensive warranty on every unit. Based on industry data, you estimate that warranty repairs will eventually cost 4% of sales revenue. During Year 1 the company spent $12,000 on parts and labor for warranty repairs.

Three legal matters are also open at year end. First, a class-action lawsuit claims the blender lid is defective. The company's legal counsel says a loss is probable and estimates it at between $30,000 and $50,000, with no amount in that range more likely than any other. Second, a competitor has filed a $100,000 patent claim over the blender's motor design; counsel considers a loss reasonably possible but not probable. Third, a former distributor has filed a $75,000 claim for breach of contract; counsel considers the chance of any loss remote.

The vice president of sales (judge) believes the company should record only the $12,000 of actual repairs as this year's expense, deal with next year's repairs when they happen, and leave all three legal matters off the financial statements until a court decides them. The vice president's (judge's) sales team bonus depends on Year 1 income.

The Year 1 data is shown in the exhibits.

You must:
- Explain the matching principle and why warranty costs must be estimated in the year of the sale
- Calculate the Year 1 warranty expense and the ending balance of the warranty liability, and journalize the warranty entries
- Determine how each of the three legal claims should be reported in the Year 1 financial statements
- Journalize any year-end entry required for the legal claims and determine the total liabilities these items add to the Year 1 balance sheet
- Explain the note disclosures required and why following these standards protects the company

You will present the information to the vice president (judge) in a role-play to take place in the vice president's office. The vice president (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the vice president's (judge's) questions, the vice president (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: What happens if next year our actual repairs turn out to be $10,000 instead of the $8,000 we have left in the liability account?
If our lawyers think we will probably lose the class action, why don't we record the full $50,000 just to be safe?

solution.overview: A strong answer applies matching to accrue $20,000 of warranty expense (4% of $500,000), records the $12,000 of repairs against the liability, and reports an $8,000 warranty liability. It then classifies the legal claims: accrue the probable class action at $30,000 (low end of the range) and disclose the range, disclose the reasonably possible $100,000 patent claim in the notes only, and ignore the remote claim, giving $38,000 of total liabilities and Year 1 income $38,000 lower than the vice president's plan.

answer: Matching (expense recognition): expenses go in the same period as the revenue they helped earn
The warranty promise was made when the blenders were sold this year, so the obligation exists now
The total expected repair cost on Year 1 sales is Year 1 expense, even if repairs happen next year
Expensing only repairs paid would overstate Year 1 income and understate liabilities
Warranty expense: 500,000 x 4% = $20,000
Entry 1: debit Warranty Expense, credit Estimated Warranty Liability $20,000
Entry 2: repairs of $12,000 reduce the liability; they are not a second expense
Ending Estimated Warranty Liability: 20,000 minus 12,000 = $8,000
U.S. GAAP (ASC 450) looks at how likely the loss is and whether it can be reasonably estimated
Class action: probable and estimable, so accrue a liability now
Patent claim: reasonably possible, so no entry; disclose the nature and the $100,000 amount in the notes
Distributor claim: remote, so no entry and no disclosure
No amount in the $30,000 to $50,000 range is more likely, so U.S. GAAP accrues the minimum: $30,000
Entry: debit Litigation Loss, credit Estimated Litigation Liability $30,000
Total liabilities from these items: 8,000 warranty + 30,000 litigation = $38,000
Year 1 expenses: 20,000 + 30,000 = $50,000 vs. $12,000 under the vice president's plan, so income is $38,000 lower
Describe the warranty and show the liability reconciliation: 0 + 20,000 minus 12,000 = 8,000
Class action: describe the claim and disclose that the loss could be up to $20,000 more than the $30,000 accrued
Patent claim: describe it and the possible $100,000 loss
Accruing a loss is not admitting guilt; it reports a probable outflow so lenders and investors are not misled
Leaving known obligations out to protect a bonus is misleading reporting and hurts the company's credibility

journal_entries.description: Accrue estimated warranty cost on Year 1 sales ($500,000 x 4%)
Warranty repairs performed during Year 1 (parts and labor)
Accrue probable class-action loss at the low end of the estimated range

calculations.label: Treatment of the legal claims
steps: Class action: probable, range $30,000 to $50,000, no best estimate: accrue $30,000, disclose possible additional $20,000
Patent claim: reasonably possible: accrue $0, disclose $100,000
Distributor claim: remote: accrue $0, no disclosure

calculations.label: Total effect vs. the vice president's plan
steps: Vice president's plan: $12,000 of repairs only

judge_question_answers.question: What happens if next year our actual repairs turn out to be $10,000 instead of the $8,000 we have left in the liability account?
answer: The first $8,000 of repairs is charged against the liability, bringing it to zero
The extra $2,000 is recorded as warranty expense in Year 2
This is a change in accounting estimate: handled in the current and future periods, Year 1 is not restated
We should also review the 4% rate for future sales

judge_question_answers.question: If our lawyers think we will probably lose the class action, why don't we record the full $50,000 just to be safe?
answer: GAAP requires the best estimate; when no amount in the range is better, U.S. GAAP accrues the minimum, $30,000
Recording $50,000 would understate income and create a hidden reserve that could be used to smooth future profits
The possible extra $20,000 is still disclosed in the notes, so users see the full exposure
Under IFRS (IAS 37) the midpoint, $40,000, would be recorded instead

key_concepts.definition: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they help earn, so warranty costs for this year's sales are expensed this year.
A liability of uncertain amount or timing, such as a warranty, that is estimated and recorded when the obligation arises. Warranty expense = sales x estimated warranty rate.
The warranty cost expected but not yet paid. Ending liability = beginning balance + expense accrued minus repairs performed.
A possible loss that depends on a future event, such as the outcome of a lawsuit, arising from something that already happened.
The future event is likely to occur. A probable loss that can be reasonably estimated must be accrued (U.S. GAAP, ASC 450).
More than remote but less than likely. No entry is made, but the nature of the claim and the possible amount are disclosed in the notes.
The chance of loss is slight. No entry and usually no disclosure.
When a probable loss is estimated as a range and no amount is more likely, U.S. GAAP accrues the minimum and discloses the rest; IFRS uses the midpoint.
An update to an estimate when new information appears; recorded in the current and future periods, not by restating past statements.
Written explanations that accompany the financial statements, such as descriptions of warranties and lawsuits, so users understand risks not shown in the numbers.

notes: ICDC level because students must combine a warranty provision with the three-level contingency test, apply the minimum-of-the-range rule, and total the effect on liabilities and income while resisting an executive with a bonus at stake. Watch for students who expense the $12,000 on top of the $20,000 accrual, accrue the midpoint ($40,000) or the high end, accrue the reasonably possible patent claim, or disclose the remote claim. The warranty part overlaps the Voltra E-Bikes state practice scenario, so the contingencies part is where top students separate themselves.
corrections: Added a loss contingencies part: Gemini's title promised contingent liabilities but the scenario only covered warranties, and it duplicated the Voltra E-Bikes warranty practice scenario at a level too simple for ICDC

New contingency facts: class action probable, $30,000 to $50,000 with no best estimate (accrue $30,000, disclose range); $100,000 patent claim reasonably possible (disclose only); remote claim (no accrual, no disclosure); total liabilities 8,000 + 30,000 = $38,000
Gave the remote claim a $75,000 amount (a former distributor's breach of contract claim) so students must actively exclude it; the spec did not fix an amount
Added the journal entry Dr Litigation Loss (Loss from Lawsuit) 30,000 / Cr Estimated Litigation Liability 30,000

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the matching principle puts all expected repair costs on Year 1 sales into Year 1 because the warranty promise was made when the blenders were sold, calculates $20,000 of warranty expense (4% of $500,000), and shows the $12,000 of repairs reduce the liability to $8,000 rather than adding a second expense.
criteria.meets: Uses matching to accrue $20,000 of warranty expense and reports an ending Estimated Warranty Liability of $8,000.
criteria.below: Calculates the $20,000 estimate but also expenses the $12,000 of repairs (a $32,000 total), or cannot explain why next year's repairs belong in Year 1.
criteria.little: Agrees with the vice president to expense only the $12,000 of actual repairs, or does not address the warranty.

criteria.exceeds: Records all three entries (debit Warranty Expense, credit Estimated Warranty Liability $20,000; debit Estimated Warranty Liability, credit Cash $12,000; debit Litigation Loss, credit Estimated Litigation Liability $30,000) and explains how posting them leaves liabilities of $8,000 and $30,000.
criteria.meets: Records the $20,000 warranty accrual, the $12,000 repair entry against the liability, and the $30,000 litigation accrual.
criteria.below: Records the warranty accrual correctly but debits Warranty Expense for the repairs, or records the litigation entry at the wrong amount.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entries, or entries with unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Classifies the class action as probable (accrue $30,000, the minimum of the range because no amount is more likely), the $100,000 patent claim as reasonably possible (disclose only) and the $75,000 distributor claim as remote (ignore), then totals $38,000 of liabilities and Year 1 expenses of $50,000, so income is $38,000 lower than the vice president's plan.
criteria.meets: Correctly accrues $30,000 for the class action, discloses the patent claim without an entry, ignores the remote claim, and reports $38,000 of total liabilities.
criteria.below: Classifies the claims mostly correctly but accrues the $40,000 midpoint or the $50,000 high end, or accrues the reasonably possible patent claim.
criteria.little: Leaves all three claims off the statements as the vice president wants, or accrues all of them.

items.label: Explain financial disclosure regulations and policies

criteria.exceeds: Lists the required notes: the warranty and its liability reconciliation (0 plus $20,000 minus $12,000 equals $8,000), the class action with a possible loss up to $20,000 more than the $30,000 accrued, and the $100,000 patent claim, and states that the remote claim needs no disclosure.
criteria.meets: Explains that the class action range and the reasonably possible $100,000 patent claim must be disclosed in the notes, while the remote claim is not.
criteria.below: Knows notes are needed but discloses the remote claim or leaves out the patent claim.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounting standards

criteria.exceeds: Explains that U.S. GAAP (ASC 450) tests how likely a loss is and whether it can be estimated, that accruing is not admitting guilt, and that leaving known obligations out to protect a sales bonus would mislead lenders and investors and hurt the company's credibility.
criteria.meets: Explains that GAAP requires recording probable, estimable losses and warranty costs whatever the vice president prefers, so users are not misled.
criteria.below: Mentions GAAP or rules in general terms without connecting them to the warranty or lawsuits.
criteria.little: Does not mention accounting standards, or suggests the company may wait until a court decides.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the warranty and litigation entries to the balance sheet ($38,000 of liabilities), the income statement ($50,000 of expenses) and the vice president's bonus, showing why each classification leads to a different treatment.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from counsel's assessments to the treatment of each claim.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or treats all three claims the same way.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Firmly but respectfully rejects the vice president's plan, explains the $38,000 lower income honestly, and suggests reviewing the 4% warranty rate as actual repair data comes in.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear decision to record the $20,000 warranty accrual and the $30,000 litigation accrual despite the vice president's objection.
criteria.below: Hesitates or partly gives in to the vice president's plan.
criteria.little: Goes along with the vice president's plan.

criteria.exceeds: Explains matching and probable, reasonably possible and remote in plain language a sales executive can follow, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the warranty, the three claims, the entries and the disclosures clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple table of the three claims (likelihood, entry, disclosure) or a comparison of $50,000 against $12,000 of expense that makes the treatment obvious, and frames the standards as protection for the company.
criteria.meets: Organizes the warranty and claims in a way that makes the treatment easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: if repairs are $10,000, the first $8,000 uses up the liability and the extra $2,000 is Year 2 warranty expense as a change in estimate with no restatement; and U.S. GAAP accrues the $30,000 minimum because recording $50,000 would understate income and create a hidden reserve, while the extra $20,000 is disclosed (IFRS would record the $40,000 midpoint).
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the extra $2,000 is a Year 2 expense and that U.S. GAAP records the $30,000 minimum and discloses the rest.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or says Year 1 must be restated or that $50,000 is the safer choice.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers.

key_points: Matching: warranty costs on Year 1 sales are Year 1 expense even if repairs happen next year
Warranty expense = $500,000 x 4% = $20,000; repairs of $12,000 reduce the liability to $8,000
Class action is probable with no best estimate in the $30,000 to $50,000 range, so accrue the $30,000 minimum and disclose up to $20,000 more
Entry: debit Litigation Loss $30,000, credit Estimated Litigation Liability $30,000
Patent claim is reasonably possible: no entry, disclose the $100,000; distributor claim is remote: no entry, no disclosure
Total liabilities from these items = $8,000 + $30,000 = $38,000; Year 1 expenses $50,000 vs $12,000, so income is $38,000 lower
Leaving known obligations off to protect a bonus is misleading; accruing a loss is not admitting guilt
